Brugsch reads the stones in their own tongue, which gives his tale its force. Seymour's English prose is clear and grave. The pair was the first full past of Egypt in English from its own proofs. That feat still stands.
taylor-greeks-goths-runes-1879:
Isaac Taylor, an English cleric and writer on alphabets, put his rune theory in this book of 1879. He held that the runes of the Goths grew out of the Greek script. The claim stirred sharp debate among Victorian scholars of the north.

Taylor traced each rune sign back to a Greek form and told how the script may have moved north. He drew on trade routes and old carved finds to back his case. Right or wrong, his book was a turn in the study of where runes began. It also shows how bold the Victorian taste for grand schemes ran.
conway-demonology-devil-lore-1879:
Moncure Daniel Conway wrote Demonology and Devil-lore in 1879. Conway was a US-born priest turned free thinker in London. His two books set the Devil in the myths of all lands. It is the great Victorian work of its kind.

Serpents, dragons, and the fall of bright gods fill the first sweep. Conway traces how each faith made its own fiend from old foes. Tales from India, Persia, and the North stand side by side. The book treats the Devil as a key to man's own fears and hopes.
strindberg-the-red-room-1879:
August Strindberg wrote The Red Room in 1879, here in Ellie Schleussner's English translation of 1913. The novel that made Strindberg famous is the first modern Swedish novel in the judgment of critics. Its satirical panorama of Stockholm's artistic underworld still stings Swedish officialdom and bohemia alike in print.

Arvid Falk, a young idealist, quits a clerk's desk to write and starves among Stockholm bohemians. The Red Room of Berns restaurant hosts actors, painters, and journalists trading wit, debt, and dashed hopes nightly. Crooked companies, bought newspapers, and charitable frauds expose a city where money mocks merit at every turn. Falk's sister-in-law, his brother the shopkeeper, and a sea of spear-carriers fill the social canvas wide. Schleussner's version gave English readers the novel that remade Swedish prose fiction in 1879.
clifford-lectures-essays-vol-1-1879:
W. K. Clifford published Lectures and Essays, Volume 1, in 1879, shortly after his early death. Clifford was a mathematician and philosopher known for bold, clear thought. The volume contains The Ethics of Belief, his most famous essay. It argues that it is wrong, always and everywhere, to believe on weak evidence.

A shipowner who lets a doubtful ship sail stands as his central case. Clifford extends the duty of inquiry to religion, science, and daily life alike. Other pieces treat the mind, the cosmos, and the aims of study. The essays made him a hero of free thought. His standard for belief still frames debates on faith and proof.
salmon-horae-mathematicae-1679:
William Salmon was a London empiric, an unlicensed medical practitioner who sold remedies and wrote tirelessly on his trades. His Horae Mathematicae, seu Urania, published in 1679, is his astrological and medical miscellany. The title joins the hours of math to Urania, muse of the heavens.

Salmon packs the book with rules for charts, cures, and the choice of lucky times for bleeding, planting, and dosing. He writes for practitioners like himself, who needed the art to pay its way in the marketplace. The miscellany shows the working library of a seventeenth-century medical astrologer in one crowded volume.
mesmer-memoire-magnetisme-animal-1779:
Franz Anton Mesmer published his Mémoire sur la Découverte du Magnétisme Animal in 1779 in Paris. Mesmer, a Viennese doctor, claimed he had found a subtle fluid, animal magnetism, that flowed through bodies and could heal disease. The memoir announced that claim to the learned world.

Mesmer set out twenty-seven short claims describing the fluid, its effects, and its use in cures. He described patients who trembled, swooned, or felt relief under his hands and magnetic rods. Royal commissions later tested his claims and blamed imagination, but his methods led toward hypnosis and talk cures. The memoir is the founding document of mesmerism.
sbe-03-shu-king-legge-1879:
Volume 3 of The Sacred Books of the East appeared in 1879, edited in a series led by Max Müller at Oxford. James Legge translated the texts, which form The Sacred Books of China, Part 1. At its center stands the Shû King, the Book of Documents, a set of speeches and records ascribed to China's earliest rulers.

Speeches, charges, and counsels in the Shû King present the model kings of old China and their ministers. Legge added the opening parts of other classics and full notes on hard passages. The volume brought one of China's oldest books into a world series of sacred texts. It helped place Chinese classics beside the Bible and the Vedas for English readers.
jevons-theory-political-economy-1879:
W Stanley Jevons published The Theory of Political Economy in 1879 in its second edition, first issued in 1871. Jevons, a Manchester economist and logician, helped start the marginalist revolution. That turn rebuilt economics on the value of one more unit, not on labor alone.

Jevons argued that utility, the satisfaction a good gives, rules value, and that each added unit gives less than the last. He cast exchange and labor in math, treating economics as a calculus of pleasure and pain. Ricardo and Mill had stressed cost; Jevons stressed the buyer. His theory, with Menger and Walras abroad, remade the science, and the second edition spread it in a fuller form.
george-progress-poverty-1879:
Henry George published Progress and Poverty in 1879 in San Francisco. George, a self-taught economist and journalist, asked why poverty deepens as wealth and progress grow. His answer made the book the best-selling economics work of the nineteenth century.

George blamed private ownership of land: rent rises with progress, so landlords gain what labor and capital earn. His remedy was a single tax on land value, replacing other taxes and leaving buildings untaxed. Millions read him, and land reform movements rose on several continents in his name. Critics disputed the remedy, but the question he posed, why progress and poverty travel together, still has force.
pasteur-studies-on-fermentation-1879:
Louis Pasteur was a French chemist who proved that tiny living germs cause fermentation and many diseases. He studied why beer and wine often turned sour or spoiled. Faulkner and Robb translated his French work into English, and it was published in 1879.

Pasteur shows through careful experiments that each kind of fermentation comes from a specific microbe. He explains how brewers can protect beer by controlling those germs and by gentle heating. His results gave brewers a practical guide and gave medicine strong proof of the germ theory. The book changed both brewing and science.
lessing-nathan-the-wise-1779:
Nathan the Wise, Lessing's verse play of 1779, reached English first in William Taylor's translation of 1791. In Jerusalem under Saladin, the Jewish merchant Nathan is asked which of three faiths is the true one. He answers with the parable of three rings, each claimed as the one true ring.

Around that parable Lessing weaves Templars, sultans, patriarchs, and hidden kinship. The plot slowly reveals a family divided by creed yet bound by blood. His plea is for tolerance among Jews, Christians, and Muslims alike. The play grew from Lessing's own quarrels with church authority in Hamburg. Its ring parable remains the Enlightenment's clearest statement against fanaticism.
petrarch-sonnets-triumphs-1879:
Francesco Petrarca, called Petrarch, shaped his sonnets to Laura across a lifetime in the 1300s. The 1879 English volume from Bell's library gives his Sonnets, Triumphs, and other poems in verse by several hands. It was the first complete English rendering of the whole body of his Italian poetry.

The sonnets trace love for Laura in life and grief for her after death. The Triumphs stage grand processions of Love, Death, Fame, and Time in vision form. Petrarch's careful music set the pattern for love poetry across Europe for centuries. Shakespeare and the Elizabethans drank deeply from this source. The Bell volume let Victorian readers meet the full Petrarch, not a selection.
bustan-clarke-1879:
Captain H. Wilberforce Clarke published the first complete English Bustan in 1879, in prose, for Wm. H. Allen of London. Saadi wrote the Bustan, the Orchard, in verse in 1257, a year before the Gulistan. Where the Rose Garden mixes prose and verse, the Orchard sings its counsel in verse throughout, across ten chapters.

Justice, mercy, humility, and the dervish life supply the tales' great themes. Saadi tells of kings taught by beggars and scholars corrected by fools. Clarke, a Royal Engineers officer and Persian scholar, kept the stories plain and full. His version stood alone in English for generations. Read with the Gulistan, the Bustan completes Saadi's double handbook for living well.
al-tabari-sasanian-history-noeldeke-1879:
Al-Tabari, the great historian of Baghdad, opened his vast History of the Prophets and Kings with the ancient world and the kings of Persia. Theodor Nöldeke turned the Sasanian portion into German in 1879. His version is the chief public domain rendering of Tabari. The text recounts Persia and the Arabs in the age of the Sasanians.

The Persian kings pass in line from Ardashir to Yazdegerd, with their wars against Rome and their court tales. Beside them stand the Arab buffer kings of Hira and the tribes of the desert. Nöldeke adds deep notes on names, dates, and Persian sources. Through Tabari, the lost chronicles of Sasanian Persia still speak.
chanson-croisade-albigeoise-vol-2-1879:
Paul Meyer closed his edition of the Chanson de la Croisade Albigeoise with this second tome in 1879. The poem, in Old Provençal, is the epic of the crusade called against the Cathars of Languedoc in 1209. Meyer's edition ran from 1875 to 1879 and gave the song its modern scholarly form.

The verse runs on through the wars for Toulouse, the death of Simon de Montfort under its walls, and the slow hardening of the conquest. The second poet writes as a son of the south, and his grief and pride fill the lines. Meyer's notes, glossary, and apparatus complete the edition here. The two tomes together hold a whole people's war song.
hume-dialogues-natural-religion-1779:
David Hume wrote his Dialogues Concerning Natural Religion in his last years, and they were published in 1779, after his death. Three speakers carry the debate: Cleanthes, who defends the argument from design; Demea, who speaks for orthodox faith; and Philo, the skeptic who asks the hard questions. Their topic is the being and nature of God.

Philo presses the design argument until its likeness between world and machine wears thin. Suffering, disorder, and rival causes all enter his case. Cleanthes answers with warmth, and the dialogue never quite declares a winner. The work became the classic demolition of natural theology in English, and the most readable of Hume's philosophical writings.
kelvin-tait-treatise-natural-philosophy-:
William Thomson, later Lord Kelvin, joined Peter Guthrie Tait to write the Treatise on Natural Philosophy. Part one, in its 1879 form, was the complete work as published. Generations of physicists learned from Thomson and Tait, as the pair were known. The book carries Newtonian mechanics into the age of energy.

Kinematics, the pure study of motion, comes first and sets the terms. Dynamics follows, treating forces, work, and energy in depth. The authors insist on clear physical meaning behind every formula. Their approach shaped how Britain taught advanced mechanics. The treatise remains a monument of Victorian science. Its rigor set a lasting standard.
hering-guiding-symptoms-vol1-1879:
Constantine Hering spent a lifetime gathering drug symptoms, and The Guiding Symptoms of Our Materia Medica began appearing in 1879. Volume I opens his great American materia medica, a work his students finished after his death. Hering tested remedies on healthy volunteers and recorded every change they felt.

The symptoms are sorted by part of the body, from mind and head down through the frame. Marks show which signs Hering trusted most, confirmed in practice again and again. Prescribers prized the set as a storehouse drawn from real provings, and the first volume sets the pattern the rest follow.
hering-guiding-symptoms-vol2-1879:
Volume II of Hering's Guiding Symptoms, issued in 1879, carries the great symptom record forward. Constantine Hering had died with the work unfinished, so his students and family saw the volumes through the press. The plan stays the same: remedies in order, their signs grouped by region of the body.

What sets these pages apart is the grading worked into the text. Strong marks flag the symptoms seen most often and cured most surely, the true guiding signs. A prescriber could scan a remedy and find its heart at a glance. The volume keeps Hering's lifetime of proving work within easy reach.
allen-encyclopedia-pure-materia-medica-v:
Allen closed his Encyclopaedia with Volume X in 1879, six years after the first volume appeared. Ten volumes hold the fullest proving record homeopathy ever made, and the last one completes the alphabetical span of remedies. Timothy Field Allen could finally point to the whole archive, finished at last.

Later generations quarried the set for repertories, keynotes, and condensed guides of every kind. The raw pages remain the court behind those courts, where a claim about a drug can be checked against the provers' own words. Volume X ends the largest homeopathic materia medica ever compiled, a monument to patient gathering.
allen-encyclopedia-pure-materia-medica-i:
Allen's Encyclopaedia needed a key, and the general index of 1879 provides it. Ten volumes of proving symptoms are hard to search by hand, so the index cross-references symptoms and remedies across the whole set. A reader starts from a sign and lands on the drugs that produced it.

That makes the slim index the most practical volume of the eleven for daily use. It turns a vast archive into a working tool at the desk. Anyone using Allen's record today still begins here, since the index shows at a glance where each remedy and symptom can be found.
biruni-chronology-ancient-nations-sachau:
Al-Biruni compared the calendars of nations in The Chronology of Ancient Nations, written about 1000 and Englished by Sachau in 1879. The Arabic title, Athar-ul-Bakiya, names the signs of past centuries that survive in feasts and eras. Persians, Jews, Christians, and pre-Islamic Arabs all keep time differently, and al-Biruni lays their systems side by side.

Festivals, fasts, and New Year days get careful treatment, since a calendar is a people's memory in numbers. The book shows comparative science at a very early, very high level. Historians of astronomy and religion both draw on Sachau's version of this founding work.
kumarasambhava-griffith-1879:
R. T. H. Griffith translated Kalidasa's Kumarasambhava in 1879 for Trubner's Oriental Series, under the title The Birth of the War-God. Kalidasa, India's most celebrated Sanskrit poet, tells how the gods scheme to wed Shiva to Parvati, daughter of the mountain. Only their son, the gods hope, can kill the demon Taraka, who torments heaven and earth alike.

Parvati wins the meditating god by matching his austerity with her own, in some of Sanskrit poetry's most loved and tender scenes. Spring, the high Himalaya, and the burning of the love god blaze along the way. Griffith's verse carried Kalidasa's epic of divine courtship to English readers in graceful, faithful form.
clausius-mechanical-theory-heat-browne-1:
Rudolf Clausius, a German physicist, spent years turning heat into a branch of exact math. Walter Browne's 1879 English version gathers Clausius's key papers on the mechanical theory of heat. Together they form one of the founding books of a new science.

Clausius states the two great laws: energy is conserved, and heat flows only from hot to cold. He also coins the word entropy for the measure of energy that is lost to use. Engineers and physicists still build on the clear, strict reasoning set out in these pages. Readers also get his work on gases and the paths their particles trace.
lewis-short-latin-dictionary-1879:
Charlton Lewis and Charles Short published their Latin Dictionary in 1879, building on the work of the German scholar Freund. It became the scholar's standard Latin-English dictionary for a century and a half. Classicists still call it simply Lewis and Short.

Every classical word is given with its full range of senses, its grammar, and citations from the authors who used it. Entries trace a word from early Latin through the golden age and beyond. The detail lets readers weigh how Cicero, Virgil, or Tacitus used a term. For serious Latin reading, this remains the great one-volume authority in English.
baker-cyprus-as-i-saw-it-1879:
Samuel White Baker, the explorer of the Nile sources, surveyed Cyprus in 1879, the first year of British rule there. His Cyprus as I Saw It reports a tour of the whole island. Britain had taken Cyprus from the Ottoman Empire the year before.

Baker rides through the plains and mountains, noting farms, forests, ruins, and the island's many peoples. He judges roads, water, and fever with a practical eye and urges planting and reform. His wife Florence, who shared his African travels, was with him on the tour. The book is the first full English picture of Cyprus under its new rulers.
plos-pone-0003379:
Stella Quimbo and colleagues studied health insurance use in the Philippines for this 2008 paper. The country promotes social health insurance to help poor families get care. Yet many poor families were not using the cover they had. The team looked at use across thirty hospital districts to find out why.

Their data show that having a card does not ensure a person gets care. Costs, travel, and poor knowledge of benefits all kept people away. The paper argues that programs must fix those blocks, not just sign people up. The lesson applies to many poor countries building insurance schemes of their own.
plos-pone-0003479:
Murilo S. Baptista, Josué X. de Carvalho, and Mahir S. Hussein studied network wiring in this 2008 paper. Active networks, like neural circuits, pass information while their parts fire. The shape of the wiring shapes how much information moves. It also shapes how well the network falls into sync.

The team sought wiring layouts close to the best possible ones. Their method finds topologies that transmit large amounts of information. Such layouts link pure graph theory to working systems. Designers of real networks can borrow the same search logic. The tools apply to any network where parts pass signals to each other.
plos-pone-0003579:
Davide Lecca and co-authors studied a receptor tied to brain repair in this 2008 paper. Replacing damaged cells in the adult brain needs new neurons and oligodendrocytes. Oligodendrocytes make the myelin that insulates nerve fibers. A receptor named GPR17 had just been identified.

GPR17 resembles P2Y-like receptors that sense nucleotide signals. The team cast it as a sensor of brain damage. It also stands as a new target for brain repair strategies. A druggable sensor could help rebuild rather than just protect tissue. Brain repair has long been a goal that drugs could not reach.
plos-pone-0003679:
Lorenza S. Colzato, Wery P. M. van den Wildenberg, and Bernhard Hommel published this psychology study in PLOS ONE in 2008. Beliefs and expectations are known to shape what people see. Yet no one had tested whether a religious upbringing changes basic visual attention. The authors compared Dutch Calvinists with atheists raised in the same culture.

The groups differed in how they spread attention between the whole scene and its details. The religious participants were more prone to miss the big picture in favor of local detail. The study shows a cultural force reaching down into the basic mechanics of seeing.
plos-pone-0003779:
Michaela Petter, Insa Bonow, and Mo-Quen Klinkert published this malaria study in PLOS ONE in 2008. The malaria parasite Plasmodium falciparum spends several days maturing its sexual stages, called gametocytes, inside the human host. During that time it must evade the immune system and hide in body tissues.

The team tracked the rif multigene family, a set of variable surface genes, during gametocyte development. Different subgroups of the family switched on in diverse patterns as the stages matured. The shifting patterns show how the parasite varies its surface while preparing to infect mosquitoes.
plos-pone-0003879:
Ian P. Lewkowich, Stephane Lajoie, Jennifer R. Clark, and co-authors studied asthma in mice in 2008. Their PLOS ONE article focuses on dendritic cells in the lung. These cells take in allergens and switch on T cells, the immune cells behind allergic asthma. In asthma-prone mice, lung dendritic cells seem primed to drive that response.

The authors traced how allergen uptake by these cells leads to release of IL-23. That signal helps push airways toward overreaction, a core feature of asthma. The work names a step where treatment might calm the response. It also clarifies why some lungs react so strongly to common allergens.
plos-pone-0003979:
Dave J. Druce, Graeme Shannon, Bruce R. Page, and co-authors set out a savanna monitoring plan in 2008. Managers of protected areas need warning before vegetation shifts hard. Large trees, at least five meters tall, do key ecological work. Their loss can signal a regime shift in the landscape.

Their PLOS ONE article develops a protocol for tracking large trees. It covers both the mix of tree species and how animals use them. Repeated checks can catch change while response is still cheap. The plan supports adaptive management in African conservation areas. The work appeared in PLOS ONE, with its methods and data open for all to see.
plos-pone-0004079:
Ruth Prassl, Magdalena Pregetter, Heinz Amenitsch, and co-authors measured fat particles in blood as heat sensors in 2008. Low density lipoproteins carry cholesterol through the bloodstream. Their fatty core changes state with temperature in a sharp transition. Whether that change is fast enough to matter was unknown.

Their PLOS ONE article used sub-second X-ray measures on LDL particles. The core responded quickly to small swings of about two degrees. A fast response could let LDL sense temperature in circulation. The result gives a physical side to a familiar risk factor. The article came out in PLOS ONE, an open journal for science and health research.
plos-pone-0004179:
Priyadharsini Nagarajan and colleagues published this skin cancer study in PLOS ONE in 2009. Ets1 is an oncogene, a gene that can drive cancer, acting as a transcription factor that controls many genes tied to tumour start and growth. It is over-produced in many human squamous cell cancers, and the amount tracks with how far the cancer has advanced.

The team switched Ets1 on in fully matured squamous skin cells, which normally no longer divide. They report that Ets1 alone drives abnormal, dysplastic changes in these cells. The result shows how one over-active gene can push settled skin cells back toward a cancer-like state.
plos-pone-0004279:
Lucas Joppa, Scott Loarie, and Stuart Pimm published this conservation study in PLOS ONE in 2009. Protected areas are the first, and often only, line of defence for biodiversity. They might help or harm rural communities depending on how they change economic opportunities and access to natural resources.

Because of that, protected areas may attract or repel human settlement. The authors examine population growth near protected areas around the world. Whether people crowd toward park edges or drift away shapes both conservation planning and the lives of rural neighbours. The authors treat people as part of the landscape, not outside it.
plos-pone-0004379:
The tropics of the Americas hold more bird species than any other region on Earth. Yet how those birds split into separate species is still poorly mapped. Kevin Kerr, Darío Lijtmaer, Ana Barreira, and co-authors used DNA barcodes to probe the pattern. Their 2009 PLOS ONE paper draws on short gene tags that can tell species apart.

Barcoding lets teams sort many birds fast, without full genome work. The authors compared tags across Neotropical birds to read regional divergence. Genetic data for the region had been thin before. Their survey adds a broad base for later studies. It also helps spot hidden diversity, where two look-alike populations differ in their DNA.
plos-pone-0004479: In 2009, Akan, Sahlén, and Deloukas drew a control map of a chromosome slice. A histone map of human chromosome 20q13.12 was built. The region's switches were fully charted. The map aids disease-gene hunting today. The region links to diabetes and more ills.
plos-pone-0004579: In 2009, El-Talatini, Taylor, and Elson mapped cannabis-like signals in ovaries. Localisation and function of the endocannabinoid system in the human ovary were charted. The anandamide source was traced. The finding maps reproductive biology anew. The exact role was unclear.
plos-pone-0004679: In 2009, Norscia, Antonacci, and Palagi watched wild lemurs trading mating favors. Mating-first, mating-more patterns showed biological market fluctuation in a wild prosimian. The clever females traded leverage shrewdly. The finding maps social economics anew. The mating power is distributive.
plos-pone-0004779: In 2009, Roybon, Hjalt, and Stott found two switches dividing brain-building labor anew. Neurogenin2 drove granule neuroblast making while NeuroD1 set nerve fate. The switches split the work neatly. The study maps memory hub growth. The cell actions are coordinated well.
jewett-old-friends-new-1879:
Early tales fill Old Friends and New, under copyright of 1879. Jewett was still in her twenties and finding her voice when she wrote them. A later list of her books shows how wide her output grew, from Deephaven to The Tory Lover.

Old neighbors, summer visitors, and village oddballs people these gentle New England stories. Readers can watch a fine writer take shape page by page. Her ear for local speech, her love of place, and her pity for plain folk are all here already. The book offers a warm window on the start of a classic American career that lasted three more decades.
dante-de-monarchia-church-1879:
Dante wrote De Monarchia in Latin during his years of exile from Florence. F. J. Church turned the treatise into English in 1879. An essay by R. W. Church travels with the translation in this edition.

Dante argues that the world needs one universal emperor to keep peace and justice. That ruler, he insists, must stand free of the Pope and the Church. The Church condemned the book for that claim, and copies were publicly burned. Readers meet a grave political mind behind the poet of the Comedy. Few medieval works state the case for world order with such bold and careful logic.
froude-caesar-sketch-1879:
James Anthony Froude sketched Julius Caesar's life in 1879, and Victorian readers made it a bestseller. Froude admires Caesar without reserve, as the strong man his own age lacked. Rome's fall from republic to one-man rule becomes a gripping personal tale.

Brilliant and readable, the sketch races from Gaul to the Ides of March. Froude defends Caesar's ambition as a cure for a rotten system. Scholars faulted his ease with fact, yet the public loved him. The book showed that Roman history could sell like a novel, and it still reads as a bold, fluent brief for its hero.
rehearsall-elizabeth-stile-1579:
Elizabeth Stile stands accused in A Rehearsall both Straung and True, a Windsor witch pamphlet from 1579. Hainous and horrible acts, confessions, and executions fill its black-letter pages. Stile and her fellows were charged with killings by sorcery in one of the earliest English witchcraft pamphlets to reach the press.

Cheap print carried the scare to markets and alehouses across the shire. Examinations before magistrates give the tale its grim, vivid detail. Belief, fear, and malice braid together in the record it preserves. The pamphlet marks the birth of the witch scare in English print, raw evidence of how neighbors turned on neighbors in terror.
bracton-de-legibus-twiss-vol2-1879:
The second volume of Twiss's Rolls Series edition of Bracton appeared in 1879. Bracton's thirteenth-century treatise set English law in order for the first time, and Twiss printed it with a facing English translation. Each volume of the edition carried the vast work one stage further.

Volume 2 treats the law of persons, property, and inheritance as Bracton's England knew it. It explains who could hold land, how estates passed at death, and what rights wives, heirs, and lords held. The rules are drawn from decided cases, so the reader sees the common law reasoning its way forward. For students of medieval society, the volume is also a record of how land and family bound people's lives together.
habeas-corpus-act-1679:
England's Parliament passed the Habeas Corpus Act in 1679 to stop prisoners from being held without answers. Under the old writ, a jailer had to bring a prisoner before a judge and explain the arrest. In practice, officials had found ways to delay, move, or hide prisoners.

The act sets firm deadlines for producing a prisoner and gives penalties for officials who dodge the writ. It also bars sending prisoners to distant places beyond the court's reach. These rules made unlawful detention much harder to sustain. The statute became a model for legal systems far beyond England.
cia-0000010479:
Probable developments in Iran through 1953 are forecast in a CIA estimate dated January 1953. The oil crisis was then at full stretch, with Mossadegh in power and the shah's position weak. The estimate's task was the year ahead, not a verdict on the past.

Forecasts for 1953 had to weigh economic collapse, communist gains, and possible coups in Tehran. The real coup came that August, changing Iran for a generation. An estimate written in January cannot describe it, which is what makes the paper valuable. It records informed expectation on the edge of a famous turning point.
cia-0000012279:
Richard Helms, the agency's chief of clandestine operations, signs an undated memo to an assistant to a cabinet secretary, its year estimated as 1961. The memo belongs to the Penkovsky file's high reaches. Memos at this level moved a spy's product into the rooms where war and peace were weighed, and Helms guarded that channel himself.

The paper's bureaucratic weight is its message: the case mattered at the top. It shows a future director's hand on the file in its busiest year. For readers, it is one of the summit traces that mark how far a colonel's secrets traveled.
cia-0000012379:
The Penkovsky memoirs were heading for print, and in October 1964 the agency weighed a request to approve their publication. The colonel's story, drawn from his papers and debriefings, would appear the next year as The Penkovskiy Papers. The CIA had a hand in bringing the book out. Approval requests like this one mark its careful management of what the public could be told.

Publication turned a secret case into Cold War argument. The file shows the government's hand in the making of a bestseller. For readers, the request is the moment the spy's story was cleared for daylight.
cia-0000013679:
Italy's center-left experiment and its Cold War meaning are weighed in a CIA paper from January 1963. The experiment brought the Socialists toward government alongside the Christian Democrats. That opening to the left alarmed Washington's Cold Warriors. Italy held NATO's southern flank and the West's largest communist party, so any shift in Rome's coalitions carried weight far beyond Italy's borders.

The paper weighs the coalition's chances and its meaning for the alliance. It sorts hope from fear in the analysts' own terms. For readers, it shows Rome's domestic experiment read as a move in the global contest.
cia-0000013879: Capture and treatment of American prisoners in North Vietnam fill a CIA report dated September 2, 1967. The report joins two linked topics: how men were seized, and how they were kept. Both halves mattered to families and to officials in Washington. Papers of this sort formed the base record on life inside the northern camp system.
cia-0000014179: Security in Western Europe during President Kennedy's visit fills a CIA report dated May 3, 1963. The visit ran from June 23 that year, and the report looked ahead to it. A president abroad needed crowds watched and routes kept safe. The paper shows the agency's part in guarding a trip that became a famous Cold War tour.
cia-0000014679: A request to card a subject in an index fills a CIA file dated July 4, 1953. The index is named in short form as IACSR, and the base document is undated. James E. Harvey sent this report from Lisbon to Secretary of State William H. Seward on 13 August 1862, two days after his previous dispatch. It is Document 479 in the 1862 volume of Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs.

A two-day gap between reports signals pressing business at the post, and in August 1862 the pressing business at Atlantic ports was the Confederate cruisers. Harvey's Lisbon letters kept Washington informed of Portuguese rulings and rumors touching belligerent ships. Seward used such reports to protest, to warn, or to thank, as each case required. The dispatch is a small but pointed piece of the maritime file. In that file the Civil War was fought with notes and port rules as much as with guns.
frus-1862-d579:
James Watson Webb wrote from Rio de Janeiro to Secretary of State William H. Seward on 23 August 1862. His report is Document 579 in the 1862 volume of Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, the State Department's printed record.

Late August 1862 found the Alabama at sea and the cruiser question rising in every Atlantic capital, Rio included. Webb, never a passive observer, reported Brazilian feeling and pressed the Union's interests with his usual energy. His letters also remind the reader of a hard fact. Brazil and the United States were then the two great slaveholding powers of the hemisphere. That fact shadowed their wartime dealings. The dispatch is part of the thin but telling Brazilian file in a volume dominated by Europe.
frus-1862-d679:
The China file for this stretch closes with a letter from Secretary of State William H. Seward to Anson Burlingame, dated 1 August 1862. Burlingame was the American minister to China, and Seward's letters to him close the China file for this stretch. The letter is document 679 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1862.

With this note, the year's back-and-forth between Washington and the China legation rounds off in the printed volume. The exchange shows the two men at work: one reporting from the treaty ports, the other guiding from a capital at war. For readers now, the full run is a clear window on how the United States dealt with China in the early 1860s.
frus-1863p1-d79:
On 13 February 1863, Charles Francis Adams sent a second dispatch to Secretary of State William H. Seward. Adams was the American minister in London. The letter is document 79 in part one of the Foreign Relations volume for 1863, the middle piece of three sent that day.

Adams's mail was the Union's window on the British mind. He wrote of what the cabinet did and what the street felt, and Seward read both to plan his next moves. This dispatch holds the middle of a busy day's work. Read with its mates, it shows the legation sorting a city's worth of news into three clean sheets for a reader an ocean away.
frus-1863p1-d179: Charles Francis Adams, the American minister in London, sent this report to Secretary of State William H. Seward on 1 May 1863. It is document 179 in the 1863 Foreign Relations volume, part of the London correspondence on Britain and the Civil War. Letters on this route carried Adams's reading of British policy while Washington worked to keep Britain from backing the Confederacy.
frus-1863p1-d279:
Writing from London on 4 September 1863, Charles Francis Adams, the American minister in London, reported to Secretary of State William H. Seward in Washington. The dispatch is document 279 in the 1863 Foreign Relations volume. It appears in the Foreign Relations series, where the State Department printed the papers it sent with the President's yearly message to Congress.

Public meetings across Britain, many of them backing the Union and emancipation, formed part of the picture Adams reported. He tracked opinion as carefully as he tracked ministers. Read alongside its neighbors in the volume, it shows the daily grind behind the war's big diplomatic crises.
frus-1863p1-d379:
On 30 January 1863, Lord Lyons, Britain's minister in Washington, wrote to one of Her Majesty's consuls, whose post the printed title leaves blank. The instruction is document 379 in the 1863 Foreign Relations volume. It survives in the 1863 volume of Foreign Relations of the United States, the State Department's official record of its work abroad.

British consuls in American ports watched over British ships, sailors, and trade, and reported up to Lyons. Orders from the minister told them how to handle arrests, seizures, and protests on the spot. Seward obtained and printed such papers because they showed how British officials were directed inside the Union. The note is a glimpse of the consular network that fed the bigger fight in Washington.
frus-1863p1-d479:
On 25 April 1863 a formal note passed from Lord Lyons, the British minister in Washington to Secretary William H. Seward. Behind the formal phrases stood a live question: would Britain stay neutral, or step into the American war? Britain had not taken sides in the American war, and holding that line was the daily work of this mail.

The real subject under all the polite wording was British neutrality. Washington wanted it kept strict, and London wanted no quarrel it could avoid. For historians, the value lies in the run of the letters. Together they trace, almost day by day, how the Union kept its most dangerous foreign problem from boiling over. Readers who work through the file in order will find this letter where the clerks of 1863 left it, in the middle of the stream.
frus-1863p1-d579:
William H. Seward, Secretary of State addressed a formal note to Lord Lyons, Britain's minister in Washington on 30 June 1863. Britain had not taken sides in the American war, and holding that line was the daily work of this mail. The exchange belongs to the Civil War years, when Washington's first task abroad was keeping Europe out of the fight.

The day-to-day work was unglamorous: answering complaints, passing on claims, and keeping track of ships, prisoners, and papers. Single letters rarely settle anything here. Their worth is in the chain they form, which lets a reader watch a dispute rise, cool, and fade in real time. Alone it is one note among hundreds. In place, it is part of how a war stayed between the two sides that started it.
frus-1863p1-d679:
A second Seward letter to London bears the date 30 November 1863. It went to Charles Francis Adams, the United States minister in Britain, and it is kept as document 679 in the 1863 Foreign Relations volume. Two notes on one day hints at a busy week in Washington.

By late 1863 the war had turned in the Union's favor on the field, but Europe still held back from full trust. Seward kept Adams supplied with facts and lines to use with British officials. The reader sees that work at the sentence level. It is a short, direct record of how a government spoke to a key envoy in wartime.
plos-pbio-0020079:
André P. Gerber, Daniel Herschlag, and Patrick O. Brown surveyed RNA-binding proteins in yeast for PLOS Biology in 2004. The Puf family of proteins grabs specific messenger RNAs and controls what happens to them. The team found which RNAs each Puf protein holds across the whole genome.

The bound RNAs grouped neatly by job and by where their proteins work in the cell. That means Puf proteins help coordinate whole teams of genes after their messages are made. This kind of control is a second layer of gene management, past the on-off switch of transcription. The study shows that layer is ordered, broad, and worth mapping in other species too.
plos-pbio-0020179:
Hiroshi Arakawa, Huseyin Saribasak, and Jean-Marie Buerstedde studied antibody gene editing in PLOS Biology in 2004. Birds and mammals improve their antibodies in two ways: gene conversion, which patches in stored variants, and hypermutation, which adds random point changes. An enzyme called AID starts both processes.

The team shows that one and the same first step, a cut-like change by AID, can lead to either outcome. The cell's later repair choices decide which path the gene takes. That shared start simplifies a once messy picture. It also helps explain how the immune system builds such a wide range of antibodies. The same enzyme can cause harm when it acts in the wrong place.
plos-pbio-0020379:
Ulrike S. Eggert, Amy A. Kiger, Constance Richter, and their team screened for cell division blockers in PLOS Biology in 2004. Cytokinesis is the final split of one cell into two. The team ran two screens side by side: one with chemical compounds, one by silencing genes across the genome.

Running both at once lets each check the other. Compounds that block division point to the genes they likely target, and gene hits predict new compounds. The screen found fresh inhibitors and fresh targets together. Such paired screening is now a standard drug hunt design. It is prized because it links a working compound to its mechanism from day one.
plos-pone-0000079:
Wataru Sonoyama, Yi Liu, Dianji Fang, and a large team regrew teeth in pigs in PLOS ONE in 2006. They used mesenchymal stem cells, the kind that can form bone, cartilage, and tooth support tissues. Placed in a pig's jaw, the cells helped build a working tooth root structure with its ligament.

A living root that anchors a crown like a natural tooth beats a metal post in key ways: it can sense pressure and heal. Pigs are a strong test since their jaws and teeth are close in size to ours. The study is a step toward bioengineered teeth for people who lose their own, though much work remains before clinical use.
plos-pone-0000179:
Chen Luxenburg, Dafna Geblinger, Eugenia Klein, and colleagues published this cell biology paper in PLOS ONE in 2007. Osteoclasts are the cells that degrade bone, central to normal bone remodeling and to diseases like osteoporosis when their activity runs out of balance. The authors describe the architecture of the structures these cells build to grip bone, from podosomes to the sealing zone.

The sealing zone is the gasket that lets an osteoclast dissolve bone in a sealed pocket. Tracing how scattered podosomes organize into that ring shows how the cell assembles its demolition tool. The details matter for drugs that aim to calm osteoclasts in bone-loss disease.
plos-pone-0000279:
Sébastien Plumet, Florence Herschke, Jean-Marie Bourhis, and colleagues published this virology paper in PLOS ONE in 2007. When measles virus copies itself, it makes a short leader transcript ending in a 5-prime triphosphate, a chemical flag. The authors show this viral RNA activates the RIG-I pathway, the cell's alarm that triggers an interferon response against viruses.

Interferon is the body's early warning signal that rallies antiviral defenses. Pinpointing which viral molecule trips the alarm shows how cells detect measles. The mechanism is a general one: RIG-I watches for exactly this kind of RNA in many virus infections.
plos-pone-0000379:
Patrick Pfister and colleagues traced the history of a family of smell receptor genes in fish, in a 2007 PLOS ONE paper. The genes, called V1r receptors, detect chemical signals in the water. The team compared these genes across teleost fish, the large group that includes most modern bony fish.

The study finds that V1r genes have evolved in divergent ways across fish lineages, rather than following one shared path. Receptor families grow, shrink, and change as species adapt to different waters and ways of life. Tracing that patchwork helps explain how animals fine-tune their sense of smell over evolutionary time.
plos-pone-0000479:
Anan Yaghmur and colleagues tuned the properties of oily membranes with custom-made peptides, reporting in PLOS ONE in 2007. Monoolein bilayers are fat films used to model cell membranes and to grow membrane protein crystals. The team added designer lipid-like peptide surfactants, small molecules built to sit in the film, and measured changes in curvature and stability.

Membrane curvature decides many cell events, from vesicle budding to fusion. A dial that adjusts curvature in a model film gives researchers new control. They can use it in basic studies. They can also use it when crystallizing proteins for structure work. The paper is a piece of soft-matter engineering with biological tools.
plos-pone-0000579:
Christian Iseli and colleagues tackled a string-search problem at genome scale, in a 2007 PLOS ONE paper. Biologists constantly search genome sequences for short words: binding sites, primers, and short reads all require finding brief sequences fast. The team presented indexing strategies for rapid searches of short words in genome sequences.

Indexing pre-organizes the genome so searches that would take hours take seconds. Short words are the hardest case because they occur millions of times. Efficient strategies here underpin the alignment tools of the sequencing era, and the paper appeared just as short-read data began to flood in.
plos-pone-0000679:
André Catic, Edda Fiebiger, Gregory A. Korbel and colleagues screened for enzymes that react with a ubiquitin-like protein, in PLOS ONE in 2007. Ubiquitin tags proteins for recycling and other fates, and a family of ubiquitin-like molecules resembles it in sequence, structure, or function. One member, ISG15, rises strongly after type I interferon, an immune alarm signal.

The enzymes sought are deubiquitinases, which remove such tags, but ones that cross-react with ISG15. Cross-reactivity matters because tag removal controls how long signals last. A screen that names the enzymes handling ISG15 gives immunologists new handles on the interferon response and its regulation.
plos-pone-0000779:
Onno J. de Boer, Jelger J. van der Meer, Peter Teeling and colleagues counted regulatory T cells inside human artery plaques, in PLOS ONE in 2007. T cell driven inflammation contributes to atherogenesis, the building of plaques, and to the onset of acute cardiovascular disease. Effector T cells are kept in check by regulatory T cells, a specialized subset. Nothing was known about their presence inside lesions themselves.

Staining for the marker FOXP3, the team found low numbers of regulatory T cells at all developmental stages of atherosclerotic lesions. Few peacekeepers amid many attackers fits a story of unchecked inflammation. Boosting those regulators is one idea this census supports.
plos-pone-0000879:
Stephane Aris-Brosou tackled the problem of dating family trees with molecular clocks, in a 2007 PLOS ONE methods article. DNA changes over time, so in theory it can date when species split. In practice, rates of change and split times cannot both be read straight from the data, so every method must assume something first.

Aris-Brosou proposes hybrid local clocks, which let rates vary across parts of a tree in a mixed way. The aim is more honest dates for when groups parted. Better dating underpins work on how species spread, how diseases emerge and how fast evolution runs in different lines.
plos-pone-0000979:
Mizuki Azuma, Lisa Embree, Hatem Sabaawy and colleagues studied a sarcoma gene's normal job in zebrafish embryos, in PLOS ONE in 2007. The gene, Ewsr1, is broken and fused to other genes in Ewing sarcoma and several other cancers. What the healthy gene does in a growing body was far less known.

Working in zebrafish, the team tie Ewsr1 to mitotic integrity, clean cell division, and to the survival of proneural cells, young cells bound to become neurons. A cancer gene with a day job in division and nerve development makes sense of its damage when fused. The fish work gives the gene a normal context.
plos-pone-0001079:
Natalia Norden, Jerome Chave, Pierre Belbenoit and colleagues found mast fruiting to be common in eastern South American trees, in PLOS ONE in 2007. Mast seeding, many trees fruiting heavily in the same year, was thought rare in the tropics. Tropical climates vary less, and fruit eaters there tend to eat widely, both arguing against synchronized feasts.

Earlier tests rested on only a few tropical data sets. With wider data, the team report mast fruiting is a frequent strategy among woody species there. A frequent strategy needs a different explanation than a rare one. The result also matters for forests' animal communities, which ride those feast and famine cycles.
plos-pone-0001179:
Cloning a full gene is often blocked by introns, the non-coding stretches that split genes into pieces. Genes that exist in very few copies pose a second problem. Xiaoping An and colleagues present a shortcut in a 2007 PLOS ONE article. Standard PCR, the workhorse copying method, usually cannot amplify a complete gene straight from genomic DNA in eukaryotes.

The authors describe rapid assembly of multi-exon cDNA directly from genomic DNA. Their method stitches the coding pieces together without the usual intermediate steps. A reliable shortcut like this saves time for any lab that needs the working copy of a gene rather than the raw genomic version.
plos-pone-0001279:
Ovarian cancer is the second most common gynecologic cancer and has its highest death rate, largely because it is found late. Anne Estep, Chana Palmer, and Frank McCormick analyzed mutations in three genes across 15 ovarian cancer cell lines, in a 2007 PLOS ONE article. The genes are BRAF, MEK1, and MEK2, links in one growth-signaling chain.

Cancer arises from accumulated mutations in critical genes, and the chain these genes form is a drug target in other cancers. The authors examine how often these mutations occur in ovarian lines and what that implies for therapy. Knowing which tumors carry them guides the use of pathway-blocking drugs.
plos-pone-0001379:
Philip Hill and colleagues published a 2008 PLOS ONE study on tuberculosis, or TB, in The Gambia. People who live with a TB patient face a high risk of catching the disease. The team followed such close contacts over time. They wanted to know how often new cases arose and which tests best flag who is at risk.

Contacts were checked with a blood test and with the classic skin test. The authors then tracked who went on to develop TB. Their data weigh how well each test predicts real illness ahead of time. Such data can help clinics focus care and drugs on the contacts who need them most.
plos-pone-0001479:
Ashok Hegde and colleagues wrote a 2008 PLOS ONE study on pancreas faults in zebrafish. A gene called mind bomb is needed to switch on the Notch path, a core growth signal. Fish with faults in this gene show pancreas flaws of unlike weight. The team read gene use across the genome in these fish.

By sorting fish by how grave the flaw was, they flagged genes that track with the flaw. Those genes are likely to answer to Notch in the pancreas. The list gives labs fresh leads on how the pancreas forms. It may also bear on human pancreas ills with Notch links.
plos-pone-0001579:
Aymé Spor and co-authors published a 2008 PLOS ONE study on two life plans in yeast. Some yeast strains eat fast and breed fast, like the grasshopper of fable. Others eat slow, store more, and live lean, like the ant. The team asked how much of that split is gene based and how much is set by the food at hand.

By growing many strains on set foods, they split the gene share from the food share. Both shares proved large. The yeast case gives a clean lab model for a deep life trade off. It may hint at why species split into fast and slow life plans.
plos-pone-0001679:
Charles J. Limb and Allen R. Braun scanned the brains of jazz pianists as they improvised, in a 2008 PLOS ONE research article. The team wanted the neural basis of spontaneous musical performance, creativity as it happens. Professional jazz pianists played inside an MRI scanner under two setups that differed widely in how complex the music was.

By comparing improvisation with playing set pieces, the authors mapped which brain areas switch on or off when musicians create on the spot. The full text gives the scan design, the brain regions involved, and how the patterns changed with complexity. The work gives a rare look at the brain in a creative state. It also speaks to how training lets artists shut down self-monitoring while they play.
plos-pone-0001779:
Daniel G. Wootton, Hyginus Opara, Giancarlo A. Biagini, and their co-authors ran a malaria drug dosing trial in a 2008 PLOS ONE research article. The aim was to find the right dose of artesunate to pair with chlorproguanil-dapsone, sold as Lapdap, a fixed-dose drug for uncomplicated Plasmodium falciparum malaria. Dosing matters: too little fails to cure and breeds resistance, too much adds side effects.

The open-label trial compared Lapdap alone against Lapdap with three different artesunate doses. The full text gives the cure rates and safety results for each arm. Combination therapy is the global standard for falciparum malaria, so dose-finding trials like this one write the recipe that clinics follow.
plos-pone-0001879:
Nan Chiang and co-authors asked whether drugs that numb pain can also change how swelling heals, in a 2008 PLOS ONE study. Local and inhaled numbing drugs are used in surgery each day around the world. Yet no one knew if they alter the calm, ordered steps by which acute swelling fades on its own.

The team tested lidocaine, a widely used local drug, along with a common inhaled one. They tracked how each drug changed the close of a swelling episode in their model. The question matters for care after surgery, since slow healing can mean more pain and more risk. Readers get an early look at a side effect few had thought to check.
plos-pone-0001979:
Anthony Wilson, Guy Teugels, and Axel Meyer traced the odd past of herring in an African lake, in a 2008 PLOS ONE study. Lake Tanganyika, the oldest of the African Great Lakes, holds a fauna so sea-like that early workers thought the lake once joined the ocean. Earth studies later showed no such link.

The team studied the lake's freshwater herring and their kin. As the title states, these fish are the product of a marine invasion into West Africa, followed by a move into fresh water. Their family tree solves a long puzzle about how sea fish came to live in a deep inland lake.
plos-pone-0002079:
Woonbok Chung and co-authors hunted new tumor markers by scanning DNA tags in three cancers, in a 2008 PLOS ONE study. In cancer, genes are often shut by hypermethylation, extra chemical tags on DNA. Those tags can serve as markers of disease and can point to genes that drive it. The team used a method that amplifies tagged CpG islands, the tag-rich stretches near genes.

They applied unbiased methylation profiling to prostate, colon, and breast cancers. New markers found this way could one day screen for these cancers or track them in blood. The prostate arm of the work anchors the method in a cancer with few early signs.
plos-pone-0002179:
Chrissa Kioussi and Michael Gross wrote a methods paper in PLOS ONE in 2008 on building network models of how body patterns form. Networks of transcription factors, proteins that switch genes on and off, lie beneath pattern formation in animals with many cells. Drawing and reading these networks in mammals is a central problem for development, brain science, and regenerative medicine.

The authors lay out how to construct such models step by step. A good model turns long lists of genes into a map of who controls whom as tissues take shape. Their guide helps other labs turn raw gene data into testable pictures of how an embryo builds itself.
plos-pone-0002279:
Adam Schikora, Alessandro Carreri, Emmanuelle Charpentier, and co-authors showed that a food-poisoning bacterium can live inside plant tissues, in a 2008 PLOS ONE paper. Salmonella typhimurium on raw vegetables and fruit is a major source of human infection, and salmonellosis is the most spread food poisoning worldwide. The bacterium was usually treated as mere surface dirt on plants.

The team found that Salmonella overcomes the plant Arabidopsis thaliana's innate immune defenses and takes up life inside the plant. A germ hiding inside produce cannot be washed off, which changes how food safety must think about fresh vegetables.
plos-pone-0002379:
Galli joined co-authors to publish a research article in PLOS ONE in 2008. Named on the byline are Soledad Galli, Valeria Gabriela Antico Arciuch, Cecilia Poderoso, among others. Its subject is tumor Cell Phenotype Is Sustained by Selective MAPK Oxidation in Mitochondria. Mitochondria are major cellular sources of hydrogen peroxide (H 2 O 2).

The writing stays close to the facts the team had in hand when the work was done. It stands as one careful step in a longer line of work, with its question and approach laid out in full. PLOS ONE is an open journal, and the full text can be read free by anyone who wants to check the work.
plos-pone-0002479:
Riba led the team behind a 2008 research article in PLOS ONE. Named on the byline are Jordi Riba, Ulrike M. Krämer, Marcus Heldmann, among others. Its subject is dopamine Agonist Increases Risk Taking but Blunts Reward-Related Brain Activity. The use of D2/D3 dopaminergic agonists in Parkinson's disease (PD) may lead to pathological gambling.

The authors lay out their aims in clear terms and keep the focus on the work itself. In short, the piece gives a clear, short route into a field that can seem hard to enter from the outside. PLOS ONE is an open journal, and the full text can be read free by anyone who wants to check the work.
plos-pone-0002579:
Snaddon and other authors present their study in a 2008 PLOS ONE article. Named on the byline are Jake L. Snaddon, Edgar C. Turner, William A. Foster, among others. Its subject is children's Perceptions of Rainforest Biodiversity: Which Animals Have the Lion's Share of Environmental Awareness?. Globally, natural ecosystems are being lost to agricultural land at an unprecedented rate.

This land-use often results in significant reductions in abundance and diversity of the flora and fauna as well as alterations in their composition. The writing stays close to the facts the team had in hand when the work was done. For science readers, it shows how a small, well framed question can add a firm piece of knowledge to a much larger field.
plos-pone-0002679:
Bertran Auvert and co-authors reported work in PLOS ONE in 2008. Their subject was estimating the resources needed and savings anticipated from Roll-Out of adult male circumcision in Sub-Saharan africa. The full author list in the catalog record begins with Bertran Auvert, and the article appeared in the open journal PLOS ONE.

The abstract states the starting point plainly. Trials in Africa indicate that medical adult male circumcision (MAMC) reduces the risk of HIV by 60%. It goes on to note a further point. MAMC may avert 2 to 8 million HIV infections over 20 years in sub-Saharan Africa and cost less than treating those who would have. Readers get a clear record of the question, the approach named in the abstract, and the context the authors give for the work.
plos-pone-0002779:
Carmen Chak-Lui Wong and co-authors reported work in PLOS ONE in 2008. Their subject was deleted in liver cancer 1 (DLC1) negatively regulates Rho/ROCK/MLC pathway in hepatocellular carcinoma. The catalog record names Carmen Chak-Lui Wong first among the authors, and the source is the open journal PLOS ONE.

The abstract states the starting point plainly. Deleted in liver cancer 1 (DLC1), a member of RhoGTPase activating protein (GAP) family. The piece stands as a short, open record of the research question and the grounds on which the authors pursued it. No results or figures are claimed in this summary beyond what the title and abstract themselves state.
plos-pone-0002879:
Shehre-Banoo Malik, Arthur W. Pightling, Lauren M. Stefaniak and colleagues searched the genome of Trichomonas vaginalis in 2008 for genes tied to meiosis. Meiosis is the cell division that makes sex cells, and it marks true sexual reproduction. How widely it occurs among tiny single-celled eukaryotes was still unclear.

Writing in PLOS ONE, the team first built a wider list of conserved meiosis genes from animals, fungi, and plants. They then looked for those genes in this parasite. Finding an expanded set present counts as evidence for sex in the organism, which changes how its spread and variation can be understood.
plos-pone-0002979:
Kristin Hartmann, Claus Bruehl, Tatyana Golovko and co-authors studied fast adjustment of inhibition in brain circuits in 2008. Activity in the central nervous system shifts rapidly, so the balance between excitation and inhibition must adapt constantly. The mechanisms behind fast adaptation were largely unclear.

Writing in PLOS ONE, they link homeostatic plasticity of inhibition to activity-dependent vesicular filling, how much transmitter is packed into release bubbles. Chronic changes in activity reshape that packing. The work offers a concrete mechanism for how inhibitory synapses keep pace with a changing network. Full methods, data, and references appear in the complete article for readers who want more detail.
plos-pone-0003079:
Matthias Dehmer, Stephan Borgert and Frank Emmert-Streib derived entropy bounds for hierarchical networks in 2008. Their paper starts from a recently introduced measure of topological entropy for non-hierarchical networks. Entropy here gauges a network's structural complexity in a single number.

The authors provide bounds for estimating the entropy of hierarchical graphs, networks built in layers. Bounds give a fast range without full computation. Published in PLOS ONE, molecular networks are often layered, so the result serves systems biology as well as pure graph theory. The complete article sets out the methods and data behind each claim in full.
plos-pone-0003179:
Barry S. Taylor, Jordi Barretina, Nicholas D. Socci and colleagues work on finding functional copy-number changes in cancer in this 2008 PLOS ONE paper. Understanding cancer at the molecular level requires mapping its genetic defects. DNA microarray tools can give detailed raw data about chromosome aberrations in tumour samples. Computer analysis is then needed to deduce actual amplifications and losses from that raw signal.

The authors address that analysis step and which copy-number alterations are functional. Readers see the gap between raw array data and usable cancer genetics. Better deduction from arrays helps labs focus on changes that likely drive tumour growth.
plos-pone-0003279:
Frédéric J. J. Chain, Dora Ilieva and Ben J. Evans test cross-species microarray use in this 2008 PLOS ONE paper. Prefabricated expression microarrays are currently available for only a few species, but methods have been proposed to extend their application to comparisons between divergent genomes. The team demonstrate limits of using hybridization intensity of genomic DNA as a basis for such work.

Their subject is single-species microarrays and comparative transcriptomics. Readers learn caution about stretching a tool built for one genome across distant species. That matters for wildlife genetics, where custom arrays for each species are rarely affordable.
plos-pone-0007379: The gene NR2E3 acts as a master switch that guides developing eye cells toward becoming light-sensing photoreceptors. In people, mistakes in this gene can cause inherited retinal disorders such as enhanced S-cone syndrome. This study shows that changes in the gene's DNA-binding region weaken its ability to pair up with itself and to team up with the protein CRX, offering a clue to how the mutations damage vision.
plos-pone-0007479: As a mouse egg matures, it clears out old genetic messages — but not all versions of a message are cleared equally. By reading individual probes on gene-activity chips instead of whole genes, this study caught that specific variants of messages degrade at different rates. The finer view shows the egg selectively trims its molecular library as it prepares for fertilization.
plos-pone-0007579: Newborns may recognize their mothers by smell before they can see. This study exposed three-day-old babies to secretions from the small glands around the nipple, collected from unrelated nursing women. The infants responded selectively and automatically to the scent, suggesting these glands send a chemical signal that guides newborn behavior.
plos-pone-0007679: Channelrhodopsin-2, a light-sensitive protein from algae, could restore sight if delivered to the retina's output cells. This study created rats carrying the gene under a neuron-specific promoter and tested how their visual system responded to light. The results check whether the engineered rats' eyes behave well enough to serve as a model for vision-restoring therapy.
plos-pone-0007779: Mixed tissue samples got a sorting trick. A 2009 PLOS ONE study by Disset's team split tissue compartments to sharpen biomarker hunts. Mixed cells blur gene readouts. The compartment trick was validated. The trick feeds diagnostics.
plos-pone-0007879: Caspase-8 is famous as an executioner of cell death, but its death-effector domains do something else: they push cells to mature. This study showed those domains drive terminal differentiation, linking the machinery of dying to the machinery of growing up. The dual use reveals how tightly development and death are intertwined.
plos-pone-0007979: Newly sequenced microbes arrive with thousands of mystery genes. This paper describes gene-context analysis tools in the Integrated Microbial Genomes system, which predict gene function from neighboring genes — guilt by association. Context, not just sequence similarity, becomes a clue to what a gene does.
plos-pone-0008079: When RNA viruses invade, cells sound the alarm through two pathways — NF-κB and IRF3. This study found that a spliced variant of the IKKγ protein decides which pathway gets used during infection. The splice variant acts as a switchboard operator, routing the antiviral response down one track or the other.
plos-pone-0008179: A hormone-resistance syndrome got a cell-screening plan. A 2009 PLOS ONE study by Szafran's team screened androgen-receptor mutants cell by cell. Faulty receptors derail male development. The screening plan was run. The plan feeds personalized medicine.
plos-pone-0008279: The Ste20 kinase family touches many cell processes, but its targets were mostly unknown. This study ran a biochemical genomics screen in yeast to find what Ste20p phosphorylates, then used the results to predict new substrates computationally. The screen-to-prediction pipeline maps a busy enzyme's clientele.
plos-pone-0008379: Human natural killer cells fight tumors, but studying them needs a human-like host. This study developed functional human NK cells in immunodeficient mice that protected against tumor challenge. The humanized model brings cancer immunology to life.

Franz Anton Mesmer, a German doctor working in Paris, published his Mémoire on animal magnetism in 1779. It is the founding text of mesmerism. Mesmer claimed to have found an unseen fluid that flows through all living things and governs health.
